items.attachmentSummary: ShowMe | Quick Preview of Tonight’s March Board Meeting. 1-We will have elementary students leading our Pledge of Allegiance. 2-We will celebrate a Barnwell Robotics Team for winning State. 3-We will approve and sign the negotiated contract with our teachers union FHEA. 4-We will vote to approve accepting bids for different pavement and roofing projects. 5-We will listen to the results of our Workplace Culture Survey and discuss next steps to make Francis Howell better for everyone. 6-We will have a second reading and vote on Policy 6310, which largely refers to the standards we use when purchasing books for the Libraries. Note: Parents have and will continue to have the power to choose the books they want their students to be able to access. 7-We will vote on a Safe Schools Curriculum developed by FHSD that is connected to K-12 Missouri Learning Standards. 8- We will have our monthly finance report where we see the big picture financial health of the district. This report will include information for board members about the possible loss of $4 million in Year One and $54 million loss over five years if Prop RT passes. You are welcome to join us tonight or watch us online at our Francis Howell YouTube channel. | xJdKPffK.com

items.attachmentSummary: ShowMe | California teachers can no longer hide children’s gender identities from their parents following a permanent injunction issued Monday in a class action lawsuit. The lawsuit was filed by teachers who felt a moral duty to protect children and strongly objected to being dishonest with parents about their kids, as the state’s “Parental Exclusion Policies” required them to do. Several California Department of Education policies were “designed to create a zone of secrecy around a school student who expresses gender incongruity,” according to the court order, preventing teachers and school staff from sharing vital information with parents. “Today’s incredible victory finally, and permanently, ends California’s dangerous and unconstitutional regime of gender secrecy policies in schools,” Paul M. Jonna, special counsel at Thomas More Society, which represented the teachers and parents in the lawsuit, said in a statement following the decision. “The Court’s comprehensive ruling -- granting summary judgment on all claims -- protects all California parents, students, and teachers, and it restores sanity and common sense. With this decisive ruling from Judge Benitez, all state and local school officials that mandate gender secrecy policies should cease all enforcement or face severe legal consequences.” The case explored four questions: * Whether the Fourteenth Amendment’s substantive due process clause provides parents a right to access information about their child’s gender identity * Whether the First Amendment’s free exercise of religion clause does the same * Whether the First Amendment provides religious teachers “a right to provide gender information to parents” based on free exercise protections * Whether the First Amendment provides public school teachers “a right to communicate accurate gender information to parents” based on free speech protections “In each case, this Court concludes that, as a matter of law, the answer is ‘yes,’” Bush-appointed U.S. District Court Judge Roger Benitez wrote in his 52-page opinion. “Parents have a right to receive gender information and teachers have a right to provide to parents accurate information about a child’s gender identity.” Under Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, California in 2024 became the first state to bar schools from requiring staff to notify parents if a child requests a name or pronoun change, seeks access to opposite-sex facilities, or attempts to join opposite-sex sports teams. State education code permits athletes to participate on whichever team is “consistent with his or her gender identity,” and California’s Civil Rights Act further includes “gender identity” under its definition of sex. “Parental involvement [is] essential to the healthy maturation of schoolchildren,” the court opinion said. “California’s public school system parental exclusion policies place a communication barrier between parents and teachers.” “Although as stated previously, the State’s desire to protect vulnerable children from harassment and discrimination is laudable, the parental exclusion policies create a trifecta of harm: they harm the child who needs parental guidance and possibly mental health intervention to determine if the incongruence is organic or whether it is the result of bullying, peer pressure, or a fleeting impulse,” the order continued. “They harm the parents by depriving them of the long-recognized Fourteenth Amendment right to care, guide, and make health care decisions for their children, and by substantially burdening many parents’ First Amendment right to train their children in their sincerely held religious beliefs. And finally, they harm teachers who are compelled to violate the sincerely held beliefs and the parent’s rights by forcing them to conceal information they feel is critical for the welfare of their students.” All content created by the Daily Caller News Foundation, an independent and nonpartisan newswire service, is available without charge to any legitimate news publisher that can provide a large audience. items.bodyText: HAPPY PARENTAL RIGHTS MONTH! On June 1, 1925, the U.S. Supreme Court issued one of the most important parental rights decisions in American history: Pierce v. Society of Sisters. The Court affirmed a principle that still matters today: "The child is not the mere creature of the State." More than a century later, parents across the country continue to advocate for a voice in their children's education and future. As we celebrate Parental Rights Month, consider supporting the work of educating, equipping, and engaging parents nationwide. Thanks to a generous partner, every donation made through June 30 will be matched dollar-for-dollar up to $40,000. https://www.momsforliberty.org/june-26-matching-grant/ #ParentalRightsMonth #WeTheParents #Moms4Liberty See less

items.bodyText: ARREST MADE: Fox Middle School teacher, Zachery Robert Leonard, 42, of St. Louis has been arrested and charged following an investigation into inappropriate sexual and criminal conduct involving a student under 14. Arnold Detectives along with School Resource Officers began an immediate investigation after the incident was reported on 5/6/2026. Leonard was initially arrested on 5/6/2026 but released as Detectives continued to gather evidence. On 5/11/2026 Detectives submitted a Probable Cause Statement to the Prosecuting Attorney's Office. On 5/14/2026 a No Bond Warrant was issued for Leonard's arrest and Arnold Detectives were able to locate and take him into custody without incident. Leonard has been charged with Enticement of a Child, (2x) Child Molestation 3rd Degree, and (2x) Sexual Contact w/ Student. Leonard is currently being held at the Arnold Police Department Jail without bond. We would like to thank the Fox-C6 School District for their cooperation and assistance with this investigation. We would also like to thank the Jefferson County Prosecuting Attorney's Office for moving quickly to file charges in this case. Our priority is the safety and protection of children in our community. The actions alleged in this case represent a serious breach of trust and we will continue to work closely with prosecutors to ensure accountability. See less

items.bodyText: Teacher wins $650,000 lawsuit after refusing to use trans students’ preferred pronouns A former Indiana music teacher has been awarded a $650,000 settlement following a long-running legal dispute with his school district over classroom pronoun use. The case began in 2017 when the teacher said his religious beliefs prevented him from using students’ preferred pronouns, leading to a policy conflict with school administrators and eventually a civil rights lawsuit. In response, the teacher adopted a last-name-only approach for all students as a compromise. However, some students reported feeling singled out and uncomfortable, prompting the school district to withdraw the arrangement. The disagreement escalated, ultimately resulting in the teacher’s resignation and years of legal proceedings over claims of religious discrimination. The settlement concludes a seven-year case that has drawn national attention to the balance between religious rights and student inclusion in schools. The outcome reflects ongoing legal debates in the United States over how institutions handle conflicts between personal beliefs and policies designed to support diverse student identities. #fblifestyle #photography #community #Education #LegalCase #USSchools References: BBC News: Coverage on education and religious rights cases Reuters: Reports on US civil rights and school disputes CNN: Analysis of pronoun policies in schools Fox News: Legal updates on education-related lawsuits See less

items.attachmentSummary: ShowMe | Becky Hormuth and her transgender son, Levi, thought they were protected after a Missouri law banning transition-related care for minors took effect in August. The law grandfathered in those who had already been receiving puberty blockers or hormone therapy prior to Aug. 28, meaning they, in theory, would be able to continue their treatment. However, the hospital where Levi had been receiving care informed patients in September that it would no longer be providing such care, citing the “unsustainable liability” the law creates for health care professionals, as it allows providers of transition-related care for minors to be sued by their patients. “We both just sat and cried together on the floor of his bedroom,” Becky said of the reaction she and Levi had upon hearing the news. “He connected with those doctors, and they’re like family to us — they know him personally. His big worry was, ‘Who’s going to help me now?’” ​​More than 500 state bills targeting lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and queer people have been introduced in 2023, according to a tally by the American Civil Liberties Union. Of those bills, 75 became law, according to an NBC News analysis of the ACLU’s data. Read more: nbcnews.app.link/xHnIJsCtDFb | WdaypvBaRA.com

items.attachmentSummary: ShowMe | The Supreme Court has ruled that parents cannot be forced to have their young children participate in school lessons that conflict with their sincerely held religious beliefs. The Court said schools must allow families to opt their children out of certain elementary classroom materials involving LGBTQ themes when those materials contradict their faith. The case arose after a Maryland school district removed opt-out options and stopped notifying parents about the content being taught. The ruling does not ban the material itself, but it affirms a foundational principle: parents — not the state — have the primary responsibility for directing the moral and religious upbringing of their children. Schools may teach these topics, but they cannot compel participation from students whose families object on religious grounds. | UOoAA.com

items.bodyText: Student Walk out UPDATE- Email from the district: let’s hope they follow their own rules February 12, 2026 FHN families: Some FHN students made the decision to leave their classes after 3rd period and walk out of the school building. FHN administrators are with the students and are directing students to move to a supervised location on campus. We are being told the walkout is a demonstration against recent actions by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The District has provided guidance to all schools for navigating student protests. Our ultimate goal is to maintain a safe and secure school campus and to ensure that students do not present a major disruption to the learning environment. Here is some information about how we respond to student walkouts. We do not dismiss schools for walkouts, peaceful protests, or other demonstrations. Students who choose to participate in the walkout will be under adult supervision while on campus. Students will receive absence marks based on their actual attendance in each class, and they will face consequences for non-attendance or tardiness consistent with our normal procedures. Instruction will continue as scheduled. Students will not be given additional time to complete quizzes or exams that may be given during the walkout. Should a walkout happen during lunch, students who choose to participate will not be granted additional lunchtime. Consistent with MSHSAA bylaws and the FHSD Activities Handbook, students must attend school the entire day, or be marked excused by the principal, in order to participate in practices, rehearsals, or games for athletic teams or performance groups. Any verbal escalations, inappropriate behaviors, altercations, or other actions stemming from participation in the walkout will be subject to disciplinary action in accordance with the FHSD Code of Student Conduct. Students will be instructed to return to class as soon as the walkout concludes. Members of the media or general public wishing to observe or participate in the student-led walkout will not be permitted on campus during the instructional day. The principal has the authority to temporarily limit all traffic in and out, including parents and visitors, to protect student safety. Administrators and counselors will be available to assist students in processing their emotions. Every effort will be made to be consistent in our guidelines and consequences. The same policies and Code of Student Conduct that govern our work every day will also apply during any student walkouts. Thank you for helping us maintain safe learning environments for all students. FHN Admin Team See less

items.bodyText: The Missouri NEA (teachers’ union) sued the state of Missouri. They tried to stop $50+ million in public tax money from going to the MOScholars program — a scholarship that helps certain kids (especially those with disabilities or from low-income families) pay for private school, homeschooling, tutoring, or therapy. The NEA argued the funding was done the wrong way (unconstitutional) and would hurt public schools. The judge dismissed the lawsuit completely. He ruled the NEA didn’t have the legal right to sue in this way, and even if they did, the funding was legal. The money can keep flowing to the scholarships. See less

items.author: Greenwood for FHSD School Board
items.bodyText: Candidate Q&A Q: How would you address individuals of the opposite biological sex seeking access to restrooms and locker rooms designated for the other gender? A: To ensure privacy, safety, and comfort for all users, I support the implementation of single-occupancy, private restrooms and changing facilities wherever feasible. This approach minimizes potential conflicts without infringing on personal dignity. Q: Are you aware that the Bible can be taught in public schools? A: Yes, it is permissible to teach the Bible in public schools strictly as a historical or literary text, presented objectively and without promoting any religious viewpoint. However, I do not advocate for introducing such courses, as they could lead to demands for similar contradictions and other forms of ideology, creating unnecessary division. I support keeping schools free from religious or political indoctrination. Since consensus on these matters is impossible in a diverse society, the best path is to prioritize core academics over divisive topics. Q: Do you have a better solution for handling book challenges in school libraries? A: Absolutely. If a school district fails to adhere to its established policies, I propose a practical compromise: Books challenged and deemed to fall into a gray area—containing potentially explicit, age-inappropriate, or controversial content—should be relocated to a restricted section requiring explicit parental opt-in consent. This empowers parents to make informed choices without the burden of screening thousands of titles or reacting after the fact. See less

items.bodyText: Wentzville School District Settles Transgender Bathroom Lawsuit with Missouri AG Great news for transparency and parental rights in Wentzville R-IV Schools! The district has reached a settlement with Attorney General Catherine Hanaway, resolving a 2023 Sunshine Law case. The board was accused of discussing a transgender student bathroom and locker room access policy in closed sessions (June 2023) instead of openly with the public. Key points of the April 2026 agreement: • No admission of wrongdoing by the district • Acknowledges parents’ fundamental right to know about and participate in decisions affecting their children’s education, safety, and welfare • Commits to full compliance with Missouri’s Open Meetings/Sunshine Law • Requires Sunshine Law training for board members and staff • Must post a public statement about the case and settlement on the district website This reinforces that important school policies should be debated in the open, not behind closed doors. Full settlement: https://ago.mo.gov/.../State-v.-Wentzville-Settlement... What do you think—transparency wins? Share your thoughts! See less

items.author: Bryce Krawzik
items.bodyText: Matt Stolle, your argument relies on a fundamental mischaracterization of what school libraries actually provide. Equating books that feature LGBTQ+ characters or themes with explicit adult content is a common but incorrect talking point. Having a diverse identity is not inherently adult or sexual, and these books are selected by certified professionals to be age appropriate for the students they serve. Furthermore, the term grooming has a very specific and serious definition involving predatory behavior. Using it to describe educators providing inclusive literature is both factually wrong and deeply harmful to the actual safety of children.The job of a school is indeed to teach kids to read, write, and think critically. You cannot think critically if you are shielded from the reality that diverse people exist in the world. As a student in this district, I see that these books are not about bypassing parents. They are about ensuring that every student, including those from LGBTQ+ families or those who are LGBTQ+ themselves, feels seen and safe in their learning environment. Education should be about expanding a student’s horizons and fostering empathy, which are skills that help us navigate a world full of different perspectives.It is also important to remember that this is a public school district funded by and for the entire community. Public institutions have a duty to represent all citizens, not just those who hold one specific set of beliefs. While parents have every right to guide their own children's reading choices, they do not have the right to dictate what is available to other people's children or to erase the representation of entire groups of people from a public space. If a family requires an educational environment that aligns strictly and exclusively with their personal private or religious views, that is what private education is designed for. Public education, by definition, must remain a space that reflects the full human experience and respects the rights of every student to feel included.

items.author: Bryce Krawzik
items.bodyText: Carrie Johnson dismissing the lived experiences of students with a single word doesn’t change the overwhelming consensus from the American Psychological Association and the American Academy of Pediatrics, both of which recognize that children can and do identify as part of the LGBTQ+ community from a young age. Claiming that representation is wrong ignores the clinical reality that access to age appropriate, inclusive literature is a vital protective factor against the high rates of depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation that marginalized youth face when they are isolated. These books are not about adult themes but are curated tools that provide children with the language to understand their own emotions and foster empathy for their peers, which is a foundational goal of any public education system. Furthermore, public school libraries are legally and ethically obligated to serve the entire student body, not just the viewpoints of one specific group. Denying the existence of these children or removing their access to information does not stop them from being LGBTQ+, it only ensures they feel unsafe and unsupported in their own community. True education is about preparing all children to navigate a diverse world with kindness and factual understanding rather than fear and exclusion.

items.author: Libby Settle
items.bodyText: Conversations about moving towards 1:1 device pushes in today’s day and age continues to baffle me. A quick search shows districts who have had this model are moving away from a 1:1 device often transitioning from "take-home" models to "in-class only" use or scaling back for younger students.Wake County Public School System (North Carolina): The district is moving to end its 1:1 take-home program for its 160,000 students, citing unsustainable long-term costs and the need to prioritize facilities.Fresno Unified School District (California): Starting in 2026, roughly 40,000 elementary students must return their laptops to be used exclusively at school.Charles County Public Schools (Maryland): Beginning in the 2025–26 school year, the district is overhauling its technology approach by shifting to shared devices for elementary grades and restricting individual devices to in-school use only for grades 3–8.Arlington Public Schools (Virginia): This district has scaled back its iPad program, ending take-home access for certain grade levels to reduce screen time and address parent concerns.Denver Public Schools (Colorado): While maintaining some technology, the district has significantly cut hundreds of ed-tech tools to save money and reduce data vulnerability.Kansas School Districts: Select schools in Kansas have ended individual Chromebook assignments specifically to combat excessive screen time. The concerns listed in this post are valid and utilize a considerable amount of a budget that can be reallocated to school repairs, teacher retention, updated curriculums, etc.

items.author: School Watchlist
items.bodyText: EMAIL TEMPLATE To: jwelby@stdominichs.org; email@mshsaa.orgDear MSHSAA Board of Directors,As a concerned Missouri parent, I am writing to demand the immediate removal of the question “How does your child identify?” (or any similar gender identity language) from the MSHSAA Preparticipation Physical Evaluation forms.This question has no place on a sports physical form. The only relevant medical information is sex assigned at birth — period. Introducing subjective “identity” language into a required medical clearance document is inappropriate, medically unnecessary, and highly offensive to many families who expect these forms to focus on objective health and safety, not ideology.Missouri law clearly requires participation in school sports based on biological sex. This wording undermines that law, confuses the process, and erodes parental trust. It signals that biological reality is optional — opening the door to unfair competition, including boys in girls’ sports.I urge you to revise the forms without delay to reflect biological sex only. Parents across Missouri are watching and will hold the Board accountable.Thank you for your prompt attention to this critical issue.Sincerely,

items.author: Jonah E Tate
items.bodyText: School Watchlist I disagree. I think educators have to tailor themselves to each student, because each student comes from very different homes and backgrounds. When taking ed courses at Truman, this was addressed and taught. Every decision, from the curriculum to the setup of the classroom, reflects a set of values. Seeing and experiencing other beliefs around you isn’t indoctrination; it’s a part of life. By separating ourselves from one another, and labeling people different than ourselves as “others” or an outsiders we aren’t protecting these kids from having “beliefs forced on them”, we’re helping them see it as something different or wrong. it’s not the compassion jesus taught. Seeing how diverse our country and state is, is part of the beauty of the US. Embrace diversity, and it won’t feel so different. As educators we should embrace every child’s differences, and tailor our classroom and teaching styles to their needs. Whether that’s a need for a more hands-on learning with projects, a need for lunch assistance for a child, or a child feeling confused about their identity and needing a safe space. We should always give that to them because in the end, we are there for them.

items.author: School Watchlist
items.bodyText: JD Kunkler I agree full medical transitions are rare. And inattentive parents are usually the ones with vulnerable children. However, it still doesn’t make it right. There is a real institutional push to create secrecy and treat parental opposition as harm.The main route is social transition first. Schools and counselors change the child’s name, pronouns, and facilities under “affirmation” policies — often without telling parents. This isn’t theoretical. It’s documented policy in multiple states and districts, and parents have sued over it.Medical steps (blockers, hormones) are harder to hide, but pathways still exist: clinics that prioritize the minor’s identity and delay parents, one parent acting against the other, or activist networks steering kids around parental consent.Minors don’t pay for this themselves. The money comes from Medicaid or insurance in some states, activist grants, crowdfunding, or one parent funding it in secret.Calling concern over this a “dog whistle” is not accurate. This is a warning.

items.bodyText: https://www.nea.org/resource-library/educator-rights-and-political-participationEducators have strong First Amendment rights to engage in political activity on your own time and in your personal capacity.You should make it clear that you are not speaking for your employer or acting on its behalf.This is an ethics violation, regardless of individuals support for her actions. Would the same people support an employee wearing a school name badge to a Trump rally or to church? Just because you personally don't agree with it. A formal complain should be made if this really did happen.​"Local Policy & Ethics Violations​Most school districts have strict board policies regarding political activity. These policies typically explicitly forbid board members or staff from using district equipment, logos, or insignia (like badges) for partisan political purposes. If a complaint is filed, the board member could face internal censure, reprimand, or an ethics investigation."

items.author: Wayne Patrick
items.bodyText: I looked into the board conduct issue, and the claim here seems overstated. FHSD does have board-conduct and ethics policies, but the available policy language is about board members acting professionally, not acting individually on behalf of the Board, and understanding that authority rests with the Board as a body in a legal session. I have not seen a policy that says wearing a board name tag at a public community event automatically equals district endorsement.At most, someone could ask whether the name tag created confusion about whether she was there personally or officially. That is a fair question. But jumping from that to “formal review and dismissal” is a huge leap unless someone can cite the exact FHSD policy and the exact legal removal process. An elected board member attending a public, family-friendly community event is not the same thing as the district formally endorsing that event.

items.author: Greenwood for FHSD School Board
items.bodyText: Cheryl Ranum Hi Cheryl. Thank you for your thoughtful questions. I appreciate the opportunity to address them.I want to emphasize that any final decision on this matter would require careful consideration and consensus from the full board as a team. There are already established ratings, standards, and laws designed to guide the selection of books for school libraries. By consistently applying these criteria before any book is introduced into our schools, we can minimize or potentially eliminate the need for subsequent challenges, subjective opinions, or sole reliance on library professionals to make determinations. This approach would alleviate the responsibilities placed on both schools and parents, requiring only that administrators commit to upholding these existing guidelines. Importantly, it preserves access for any child whose parents choose to opt in, ensuring no undue restrictions. I see this as a balanced solution that benefits everyone involved.

items.author: Bryce Krawzik
items.bodyText: Jane Puszkar I am a student, not a 'troll in a basement.' My 'keyboard' is the same one I use to text my friends and family, complete my schoolwork, advocate for my peers, and manage my job. Dismissing my voice because of my age or living situation doesn't change the reality of the students I see every day.Regarding the library: access to diverse information is not 'indoctrination.' Many students deal with feelings they don't understand, and seeing themselves represented in literature can be lifesaving. Being LGBTQ+ isn't an 'agenda' you can talk someone into; it’s an identity. Showcasing these books is simply a reminder that LGBTQ+ people are human beings who deserve the same respect as anyone else. We breathe the same air and bleed the same blood.Furthermore, I am not the one causing division; I am responding to the division you have already created. You have publicly supported rhetoric that targets marginalized groups, including calling all undocumented immigrants 'criminals.' While legal status is a complex issue, labeling people that way ignores the fact that most are families seeking safety through a flawed and difficult system.If you truly want what’s best for all students, you should be willing to listen to us rather than insulting us. I’m out here every day living the reality of this school district. You are a horrible example of a human being and I hope one day you can come to peace with everyone aside from their ethnicity, sexuality, religion and or background. And thank you I will be having a nice day knowing I have a voice and I get to use it to protect students from people like you.

items.author: Lindsey Scheller
items.bodyText: Just FYI: when my son was in fourth grade, he had recently been diagnosed with dyslexia and was falling behind in reading. As a mom and as a teacher, I was devastated. I hired Mrs. Becky Hormuth as a tutor for him over the summer. Let me tell you some of the ways she “influenced him.” ￼She taught him a bunch of reading strategies. ￼She made him feel more confident as a reader. She convinced him that being dyslexic was nothing to be embarrassed by. She got him hooked up with high interest books that encouraged him to read more. She made it fun so he wanted to go see her, even over the summer. She made him believe that he was capable of anything he wanted to do. And now he’s a thriving ninth grader with a A in English class. This post is gross.

items.bodyText: Carrie Johnson, comparing the representation of LGBTQ+ students to "rape and murder" is a significant false equivalence. A student’s identity is not a crime, and providing books that reflect the diverse reality of our community is not "glorifying" anything it is simply providing accurate, inclusive resources for all children. Public education has always used literature to help students navigate complex themes, but equating a person’s existence with criminal activity is exactly the kind of exclusionary rhetoric that makes these inclusive resources so necessary in the first place.

items.author: Bryan Medlin
items.bodyText: The Francis Howell School District has an obligation to treat all students and staff with equal dignity and respect — and that includes LGBTQ+ students and educators who are part of this community every single day. The selective removal or suppression of content that represents certain groups, while allowing others, is not neutral — it is a policy choice, and it sends a message.One has to wonder: if this were a religious or faith-based activity, would it have even been questioned? The inconsistency in how content is treated depending on the group involved is impossible to ignore, and it raises serious concerns about whether this district is applying its standards fairly and equitably across the board.I want to recognize Board of Education member Sara Dillard, who has shown the kind of principled, inclusive leadership this district desperately needs. Her attendance at the St. Charles Gay Pride event is a powerful example of what it looks like when an elected official truly shows up for all members of their community — not just the ones it’s comfortable or convenient to support. This is the standard we should expect from every elected official, every teacher, and every principal in this district. Representation and visibility from those in positions of authority matters deeply to students who are watching and looking for someone to stand in their corner.To the rest of the district’s leadership: I am a Francis Howell graduate, and I expect better. Every child in this district — regardless of who they are or who they love — deserves to feel that their school stands with them. I urge you to examine your decisions carefully and ask whether they would hold up to a standard of true equity. The community is watching !!!

items.author: Bryce Krawzik
items.bodyText: Jane Puszkar, I strongly encourage you to look beyond your personal perspective and examine the actual consensus within the fields of adolescent psychology, medical science, and constitutional law. By labeling inclusive literature as an agenda or pornography, you are fundamentally mischaracterizing age appropriate educational resources that serve as a critical lifeline for students. To be clear, these books are curated by professionals to reflect diverse identities rather than to provide graphic content. Equating the existence of LGBTQ+ people to pornography is a harmful falsehood that ignores the reality of human identity and creates a dangerous environment for marginalized students. For a child experiencing gender dysphoria, access to this literature is a vital mental health resource that provides the language needed to understand their emotions, which is essential for healthy self regulation and development. According to the American Psychological Association and the American Academy of Pediatrics, the lack of representation and social support in schools is a direct contributor to the alarmingly high rates of depression, anxiety, and self harm among LGBTQ+ youth. Providing these books is quite literally a matter of suicide prevention and overall student safety. Furthermore, restricting access to information in public institutions often borders on a violation of First Amendment rights and ignores the fact that public school libraries must serve the entire community rather than just one specific viewpoint. These stories also benefit cisgender and straight students by fostering empathy and teaching them how to coexist in a diverse society, which is a necessary skill for the modern workforce. When you deny children the ability to see themselves or their peers reflected in their education, you are not protecting them from an imaginary threat. Instead, you are isolating vulnerable kids and creating a culture of shame that leads to long term psychological trauma. Understanding the truth requires looking at the human impact of these policies and recognizing that every child, regardless of their background or identity, deserves to feel seen, safe, and supported in their learning environment.

items.bodyText: JD Kunkler Jesus ate with sinners to call them to repentance, not to affirm their sin (Mark 2:17). Loving my neighbor includes speaking truth in love - believe it or not I do care about these people. I pray for them nightly, but I believe what they’re doing is evil and needs to be called out. It’s hard to sound “loving” on FB, especially when protecting children from age-inappropriate ideology in public schools.The School Watchlist isn’t exclusion—it’s transparency for all parents. Schools should stay neutral on contested sexual/gender issues instead of pushing one side with flags, curricula, and events. That doesn’t stop anyone from practicing their faith; it prevents schools from undermining mine and parental rights.I don’t have a planks in my eye about this —that scripture means “don’t be a hypocrite”. And parental stewardship isn’t ‘superiority’; it’s obedience (Proverbs 22:6, Ephesians 6:4). We can love people while refusing to let public institutions confuse kids on biology and God’s design.

items.author: Bryce Krawzik
items.bodyText: Matt Stolle, parental involvement is a vital part of education, and every parent absolutely has the right to guide their own child’s reading choices. However, there is a significant legal and ethical difference between a parent's right to guide their own child and an attempt to restrict access for the entire student body.In fact, the Francis Howell School District already has policies in place (such as the Library Opt-Out form) that allow parents to specifically restrict their own children from checking out certain materials or genres. This ensures that you have the "consent" and control you are asking for regarding your own family's boundaries.In a public district, the standard is to provide a broad range of professionally curated materials and then allow individual families to decide what is right for them. When one group of parents demands the removal of books entirely, they are effectively overriding the parental consent of other families who want their children to have access to those stories. By removing these books, the district isn't protecting parents; it is removing the choice from all parents. Public education is built on the idea that we can coexist with different values, and that requires keeping the library a space for everyone rather than a space limited by the preferences of a few.

items.bodyText: What are non-essential programs? In our district’s recent past, we’ve seen too much wasteful spending, so I evaluate every program by asking: Is it necessary? But this isn’t the spot for debates, and I won’t allow #agitprop here—I spot it a mile away.

items.author: Kaylee Morris
items.bodyText: Jane Puszkar I never screamed or mentioned the separation of church and state. I simply asked School Watchlist a question, but since you brought that up yourself, I’ll inform you more accurately.First, your claim that “the country was founded on Christian values” is not supported by historical records. The Founders came from diverse Christian denominations, but they explicitly rejected the idea of a government tied to any religion. After independence, there was widespread agreement that the new nation must not have an official religion, and that government must not endorse or support any church.Source: https://www.loc.gov/exhibits/religion/rel06.htmlSecond, the idea that “separation of church and state was meant to keep government out of religion, not religion out of government” is also incorrect. Thomas Jefferson, the very person who coined the phrase, stated clearly in his 1802 letter to the Danbury Baptists that the First Amendment builds “a wall of separation between Church and State.” That wall protects both directions, government cannot interfere with religion, and religion cannot wield government power or receive government endorsement.Source: https://founders.archives.gov/documents/Jefferson/01-36-02-0056Roger Williams, founder of Rhode Island, also argued that government involvement corrupts religion and that a “hedge or wall of separation” is necessary to keep the church pure and independent.Source: https://americanheritage.org/roger-williams-first-call-for-separation-of-church-and-state-in-america/Third, your suggestion that religion was intended to be part of government contradicts the Constitution itself. Article VI explicitly prohibits any religious test for public office, ensuring that government positions are open to people of all faiths or none. This was a deliberate rejection of the idea that the United States government should be Christian or tied to Christianity.Source: https://constitution.congress.gov/constitution/article-6/Finally, the Establishment Clause, mostly written by James Madison, was created because the Founders had seen firsthand the harm caused when governments endorse or enforce religion. They agreed that the federal government must stay neutral toward religion, and by 1833 every state had disestablished its official church.Source: https://constitutioncenter.org/the-constitution/amendments/amendment-i/interpretations/264So no, the Founders did not intend religion to guide government, nor did they believe the United States was founded on Christian values in any governmental sense. They intentionally built a system where religion is personal, not governmental, and where public officials must not use their government roles to promote their personal faith.If you are going to talk about the separation of church and state, you should at least talk about it accurately. These are literal words straight from our Founders and the Constitution. Please educate yourself

items.author: Greenwood for FHSD School Board
items.bodyText: Steve John Thanks for the support!It’s talked about but not nearly enough. You’re right—the conflict of interest is real. Teachers’ unions (specifically the NEA) represent many employees, yet they fund and help elect the board that negotiates their contracts and sets policy. This weakens independent oversight for parents and taxpayers. Boards exist to balance interests, not rubber-stamp one group.I spoke to one teacher while door knocking and she belongs to Missouri State Teachers Association (MSTA) — a professional association, not a full national union, so it doesn’t offer as many benefits. But she gave me hope that not all teachers are being controlled.I just learned that Ted House serves as treasurer for St. Charles County Families for Public Schools, a PAC that works closely with the Missouri NEA PAC to endorse and fund school board candidates in districts like Francis Howell. It raises legitimate questions about independence when the board is supposed to represent parents and taxpayers, not primarily union interests.

items.author: Erika Hsig
items.bodyText: Margarita Jasmine a regular church service is a worship gathering. The core purpose is religious practice (prayer, sacraments, sermon, and communal worship). It's for the congregation, oriented toward God/the divine, even if visitors are welcome.A community event held at a church (a food drive, a concert, a blood donation clinic, a public forum) uses the church as a venue, but the activity itself isn't a religious rite. The building is just the location; the purpose is secular or civic, even if there's a Christian motivation behind hosting it.I hope that helps.

items.bodyText: Ashley Goodwin Equal access matters, but a school-issued Chromebook isn’t the only (or safest) way to provide it. Proving to only families in need would be cost efficient and logical. Monitoring school Wi-Fi doesn’t cover off-network use, personal accounts, or apps students add themselves. A family smartphone is parent-controlled; a district device is not.Most classes no longer issue a full set of physical textbooks, so the backpack-weight comparison doesn’t hold. The real differences are distraction, screen time, content students can reach, and how much visibility parents actually have.

items.author: Michele Guarnieri
items.bodyText: So I don’t think you actually read that policy, or maybe you just didn’t understand it. That policy ensures that discussions of controversial or religious topics are handled in a manner that is objective, academically sound, and respectful of diverse viewpoints. And it applies to curriculum choices and classroom discussions that touch on subjects that could be perceived as controversial. Having a flag in the classroom isn’t exactly part of the curriculum or a classroom discussion. Now the First Amendment, on the other hand. I’m sure you’ve read that one in its entirety. The first Amendment not only protects people’s freedom of speech, expression and religion, but also protects people (and children) from others enforcing their religious beliefs on them. For example, caring more about a piece of cloth hanging in a classroom stating this is a safe place just because your religion doesn’t agree with it.If anyone is breaking any policies…it’s this Facebook page. And it’s crazy that this page is so upset about teachers being inclusive and safe for kids when there’s been quite a few religious leaders that have been caught as pedophiles. Maybe leave the religious stuff at home instead of a public school. Or might I suggest a private school instead? You’re making it incredibly unsafe for others in your community with your blatant hatred. hope that helps!

items.author: Amy Mallams
items.bodyText: Transgender People Are NOT a Threat to Public SafetyAnti-trans rhetoric portrays transgender people as violent, predatory, and/or hypersexual. In reality, transgender people are far more likely to experience harassment and violence than to inflict harm on others. Myths about transgender people often fall into two main categories: 1.) claims that transgender people are inherently violent 2.) claims that transgender people are sexual predators. NEITHER of these claims is supported by evidence. Instead, such false narratives distort public perception and fuel policies that put transgender communities in danger. These false narratives are not just misunderstandings; they are part of what scholars call a moral panic. Moral panic is when fear is exaggerated and directed at a marginalized group, painting them as a threat to society. Moral panics recycle old stigmas and anxieties (usually about race, gender, or sexuality) to justify discrimination and criminalization.Scholars note that moral panics often emerge as a response to social change; a way for communities to make sense of changing norms or perceived threats to traditional values. Throughout U.S. history, “protect the children” rhetoric has been used to vilify different groups: casting Black men as threats to white women,branding gay men as predators, and nowportraying transgender people as dangerous in schools and public bathrooms. These myths follow the same pattern, weaponizing fear to roll back civil rights under the guise of safety.Are transgender people a threat to public safety?NO. There is NO evidence that transgender people are more likely to engage in violent or criminal behavior than cisgender people. Research conducted on criminology and public safety consistently shows that gender identity does NOT predict criminal behavior. Studies find NO evidence that transgender people commit crimes at higher rates than cisgender people; instead, transgender people are more likely to experience discrimination and over-policing, facing disproportionate surveillance and punishment by law enforcement even when NO offense has been committed.According to the Bureau of Justice Statistics, transgender people were four times more likely to be victimized by violent crimes than cisgender people. Studies also document that transgender individuals experience disproportionately high rates of harassment, intimate violence, and hate crimes compared to cisgender people.These patterns show that transgender communities are far more vulnerable to violence, NOT more likely to commit it.These findings extend to public spaces, especially bathrooms. Studies consistently find that gender-inclusive restrooms and nondiscrimination policies do NOT compromise safety. In fact, places that have passed inclusive bathroom laws remain just as safe as they were before and had NO rise in crime or misconduct. Conversely, evidence shows that transgender people are at greater risk in bathrooms and other public facilities. Research from numerous medical, legal, and policy organizations consistently finds that gender-inclusive restrooms and nondiscrimination policies do NOT compromise safety. Many transgender people avoid public bathrooms altogether, leading to health problems, missed school, and limited participation in daily life.As Woodhull emphasized in testimony opposing Montana’s HB 121, bathroom bans do NOT make anyone safer; they increase harassment of everyone, force people into unsafe conditions, and violate basic rights to dignity and privacy. These laws and stereotypes isolate transgender people from public life, increase vulnerability to violence, and shift attention away from the real issue: transgender people’s basic right to safety, dignity, and access to public spaces.Are transgender people hypersexual or predatory?NO. Research does NOT suggest that transgender people are hypersexual or more likely to be sexually aggressive.Research shows that transgender folks are NOT more likely than cisgender people to sexually hurt or exploit others. In fact, research shows that transgender people are often the ones getting sexually assaulted. The U.S. Transgender Survey found that 47% of respondents had been sexually assaulted at some point. To put that in perspective, about 19.3% of cisgender women and 1.7% of cisgender men experience sexual violence in their lifetime. Despite being feared as predators, transgender people are far more likely to be victims of abuse and exploitation.The “predatory” framing does more than misrepresent reality: it legitimizes harmful policies and fuels harassment. Incorrect framings of transgender individuals as fundamentally dangerous or abnormal are used to justify increased surveillance of transgender people, keeping them out of certain public areas, and limiting their access to healthcare. For example, Texas Republican Senator Ted Cruz warned that allowing transgender people to use bathrooms matching their gender identity would be “opening the door for predators,” claiming that such laws would let “any man enter a women’s restroom, a little girl’s restroom and stay there.” This rhetoric directly ties trans inclusion to threats against women and children, echoing the same moral panic used against earlier marginalized groups.Rather than protecting communities, this myth perpetuates stigma and violence against transgender people. The stereotype that transgender people are hypersexual or predatory plays on long-standing fears about women’s safety. Throughout history, claims that marginalized groups were sexually dangerous have been used to justify exclusion and violence — first against Black men, then gay men, and now transgender people. Not only does this lead policymakers to overlook the needs of transgender people, but it also overlooks real actual threats to women, children, and other marginalized people.Policy Recommendations1.) Reject bathroom bans.Restricting restroom access harms public health, increases harassment, and violates basic human rights to dignity and privacy. Policies that ensure gender-inclusive restrooms and nondiscrimination protections reduce stigma, improve safety, and affirm the humanity of all people.2.) Affirm access to safe public spaces.Policies that provide gender-inclusive restrooms and nondiscrimination protections, such as ensuring access to single-stall facilities in schools, workplaces, and transportation hubs, reduce harassment and support the health and well-being of all individuals.3.) Protect dignity, privacy, & rights.Bathroom bans undermine the human rights to privacy and personal dignity. By singling out transgender people for surveillance and exclusion, they erode trust in public institutions and create unsafe conditions for everyone. Protecting access to public facilities is not only a matter of health, but also a matter of fundamental human rights.4.) Promote education & awareness.Misinformation about transgender people fuels stigma, hate, discrimination and violence. Public education campaigns, inclusive school curricula, and professional training can help counter such harmful myths. These interventions reduce prejudice, build safer communities, and affirm the dignity of transgender people. In addition, funding more research on gender diversity and inclusion can help policymakers make evidence-based decisions rather than relying on fear or misinformation.https://www.woodhullfoundation.org/fact-checked/transgender-people-are-not-a-threat-to-public-safety/

Incorrect framings of transgender individuals as fundamentally dangerous or abnormal are used to justify increased surveillance of transgender people, keeping them out of certain public areas, and limiting their access to healthcare. For example, Texas Republican Senator Ted Cruz warned that allowing transgender people to use bathrooms matching their gender identity would be “opening the door for predators,” claiming that such laws would let “any man enter a women’s restroom, a little girl’s restroom and stay there.” This rhetoric directly ties trans inclusion to threats against women and children, echoing the same moral panic used against earlier marginalized groups.Rather than protecting communities, this myth perpetuates stigma and violence against transgender people. The stereotype that transgender people are hypersexual or predatory plays on long-standing fears about women’s safety. Throughout history, claims that marginalized groups were sexually dangerous have been used to justify exclusion and violence — first against Black men, then gay men, and now transgender people. Not only does this lead policymakers to overlook the needs of transgender people, but it also overlooks real actual threats to women, children, and other marginalized people.Policy Recommendations1.) Reject bathroom bans.Restricting restroom access harms public health, increases harassment, and violates basic human rights to dignity and privacy. Policies that ensure gender-inclusive restrooms and nondiscrimination protections reduce stigma, improve safety, and affirm the humanity of all people.2.) Affirm access to safe public spaces.Policies that provide gender-inclusive restrooms and nondiscrimination protections, such as ensuring access to single-stall facilities in schools, workplaces, and transportation hubs, reduce harassment and support the health and well-being of all individuals.3.) Protect dignity, privacy, & rights.Bathroom bans undermine the human rights to privacy and personal dignity. By singling out transgender people for surveillance and exclusion, they erode trust in public institutions and create unsafe conditions for everyone. Protecting access to public facilities is not only a matter of health, but also a matter of fundamental human rights.4.) Promote education & awareness.Misinformation about transgender people fuels stigma, hate, discrimination and violence. Public education campaigns, inclusive school curricula, and professional training can help counter such harmful myths. These interventions reduce prejudice, build safer communities, and affirm the dignity of transgender people. In addition, funding more research on gender diversity and inclusion can help policymakers make evidence-based decisions rather than relying on fear or misinformation.https://www.woodhullfoundation.org/fact-checked/transgender-people-are-not-a-threat-to-public-safety/LikeReply

items.author: Karen Sieve
items.bodyText: I question your motives, Lauren, and of anyone running for a seat on a public school board like Francis Howell when you ignore the fact PropRT (originally SB 3) will hurt St. Charles County public schools, libraries, fire departments, ambulance services, and the developmental disabilities board. Given inflation and continued growth of our county and local municipalities, drastic cuts will be necessary. It’s irresponsible for you to suggest that sales taxes will not increase in the future. The money has to come from somewhere. The Governor also has plans to cut income taxes, and last year, Missouri eliminated capital gains tax. The Governor is also using state funds for private education vouchers, which I assume you, Jane Puszkar, and David Jaworski support as well given your campaigns are funded by the St. Charles Republican Party. If PropRT is passed, sales taxes will increase, and if the Governor eliminates income tax, sales taxes will skyrocket and be regressive, meaning the elderly, the poor and middle class will bear the burden of the higher prices at the grocery store. Services like haircuts, lawn care, etc. will be taxed. What about prescription drugs?So maybe you should practice what you preach about transparency so the community knows that you really don’t support public schools. Vote NO on PropRT. Save our public schools.

items.author: Cheryl Ranum
items.bodyText: For question 3 about books, I have a question about your proposed solution. Would we continue with the current book challenge procedure and add an extra category where the committee could decide to put a book in the new "restricted section"? I know it's already an option to approve books "with restrictions", but I'm not sure what the current options are for those restrictions. Or are you thinking that if one person deems a book controversial then it would immediately be moved to the restricted section? Because that seems like it would get out of hand really quickly. One parent might decide that they don't like books with black characters for example, and another parent might say that any book mentioning prayer might belong in the restricted section. So I'm mostly wondering what the guidelines would be and how it would be determined which books would be "deemed in the gray area".Like

items.author: Caroline Dungan
items.bodyText: Did Jane reply here? It says there are more replies than I can see. By out of state training, I assume you are referring to professional development conferences where there are some sessions you don’t agree with. I would assume as a UX designer you have attended at least one conference in your career. I attend a couple every year. Next month I am attending one that has about 100 breakout sessions. I received a schedule in advance and had to select which ones to attend. My employer is focused on AI initiatives, so I chose accordingly. With the couple time slots that didn’t have AI sessions, I chose things of interest to me. I didn’t choose sessions on topics that were irrelevant to my job or where I already know the subject matter at a level beyond what is being presented. A colleague on a different team with a different focus chose about 75% different sessions. Same conference, different experiences. You are talking about cutting teachers off from professional development over single optional sessions that quite frankly you could learn something from. But if you really insist that diversity is the bogeyman, you could insist on an admin review of their chosen schedule instead of taking a “burn it to the ground” approach.Like1

items.author: Christen Pierce
items.bodyText: When I had the opportunity to sit on the review committee for this video, I was grateful for the chance to participate in FHSD’s materials review process. I’m commenting here because I find it very disingenuous to claim that it was “voted to retain by a full liberal committee” when the “full committee” did not return to participate in the vote. On the day that we met to discuss and vote on the video, I was surprised to see that (still active at the time) School Board Director Jane Puszkar did not join us to discuss her concerns about the video, if she had any. It is important for our community to note that choosing not to participate does not mean conservative voices were left out of the discussion. I have five kids and I care deeply about the things they are exposed to; in this case, I do believe that retention was the right choice. If you have any genuine questions about why I voted the way I did, I’m happy to discuss my thoughts about it.

items.author: Bryce Krawzik
items.bodyText: Jane Puszkar it is important to clarify that in the state of Missouri, School Library Media Specialists are not merely individuals with a few college credits. They are certified educators who are typically required to hold a Master’s degree in Library Science or a related field. These professionals are highly trained in information literacy, curriculum support, and child development, and their primary goal is to ensure that every student has access to accurate information that reflects the diverse world we live in. Dismissing the scientific and legal reality of this issue because it challenges your personal worldview does not change the clinical facts regarding gender dysphoria or the documented necessity of representation. When you ignore the guidance of the American Psychological Association and the American Academy of Pediatrics, you are choosing personal opinion over the peer reviewed evidence that proves inclusive literature serves as a protective factor against depression and self harm for marginalized youth. Education is not a zero sum game where including one group takes away from another; it is about providing a safe and supportive environment for every single child. If you truly value the standard of professionalism you mentioned, I would encourage you to read the full context of why these resources are deemed essential by the world's leading medical and psychological experts rather than dismissing the very people dedicated to student success and safety.
